L249: Experiment. We train a 2-layer transformer on modular division ($p=97$) with an MLP classification head instead of the standard linear unembedding. A separate linear probe is trained on the same hidden states (with gradients detached). The MLP head achieves $\sim$95% validation accuracy, but the linear probe fails ($\sim$20%). Fourier analysis (Fig. cite106†2 ) confirms the embeddings lack circular structure—PCA shows scattered points rather than an ordered circle.
L250: Key finding. Across random seeds, some runs do develop (see Fig.cite106†2 ) Fourier structure—and in exactly those runs, the linear probe also succeeds. This correlation demonstrates that Fourier representations are not inevitable: they emerge when the model happens to find that solution, but nonlinear readouts permit alternatives. Linear interfaces constrain representations to be directional; nonlinear interfaces permit but do not require such structure.
L251: ### 3.7 The Self-Reference Property
L252: 
L253: A key question remains: how do we obtain $\mathbf{d}_{f}$ without supervision? Our central insight is that tokens themselves provide these directions.
L254: ###### Theorem 3.13 (Self-Reference Property).
L255: 
L256: Let $t$ be a token with associated semantic feature $f_{t}$. If $f_{t}$ is communicated through linear interfaces, then $t$’s representation provides the invariant direction for $f_{t}$:
L257: 
L258:  | $$\mathbf{h}_{t}\propto\mathbf{d}_{f_{t}}$$  |
L259: 
L260: where $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ is obtained by passing token $t$ through the model.
L261: ###### Proof sketch.
L262: 
L263: By Theorem cite98†3.7 , $f_{t}$ occupies an invariant subspace $\mathcal{S}_{f_{t}}$. Under directional invariance (Proposition cite107†B.2 ), $\mathcal{S}_{f_{t}}=\text{span}(\{\mathbf{d}_{f_{t}}\})$. Since $t$ canonically expresses $f_{t}$, its representation must lie in $\mathcal{S}_{f_{t}}$, hence $\mathbf{h}_{t}=\lambda_{t}\mathbf{d}_{f_{t}}$ for some scalar $\lambda_{t}$. Full proof in Appendix cite38†A . ∎
L264: ###### Remark 3.14 (Tokens Provide Directions).
L265: 
L266: The Self-Reference Property has a simple practical implication: tokens tell you where to look. To find the “France” feature in any representation, obtain the direction from the token “France” and project onto it. The feature is there—flowing through invariant directions by architectural necessity—and focusing on the right direction reveals it.
L267: ###### Remark 3.15 (Why “Identity-Projection”).
L268: 
L269: The framework’s name reflects this self-referential structure: projecting onto the direction provided by token $t$ focuses on $t$’s identity—the features that define $t$. The token serves as its own reference point.
L270: ### 3.8 Empirical Validation of the Self-Reference Property
L271: 
L272: Theorem cite108†3.13 predicts that token representations align with the invariant directions of their associated features. We test this by comparing each class token’s hidden state against the mean instance vector for each class, computed across attention heads.
L273: Specifically, for each attention head and class $k$, we compute the cosine similarity between the class token direction $\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}}$ and the mean instance direction $\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{k}$ for the same class (within-class) versus other classes (between-class). If tokens provide feature directions as predicted, within-class similarity should consistently exceed between-class similarity.
L274: Figure cite109†3 confirms this prediction: across 89.6%-98.6% of attention heads, the class token aligns more strongly with its own class instances than with any other class. This pattern validates the Self-Reference Property—tokens encode the same directional features present in contexts expressing those features, enabling zero-shot extraction of semantic directions.
L275: ## 4 Methods for Extracting Directions
L276: 
L277: The Self-Reference Property (Theorem cite108†3.13 ) has a practical consequence: since tokens provide feature directions and communicable features are linear (Theorem cite98†3.7 ), a classifier built on token directions should generalize to instances it was never trained on.
L278: A probe anchored to the “France” or “South Korea” direction (which we call a class token or class prompt) should correctly classify implicit prompts like “the country of the Eiffel Tower” or “the country of the Han River” (which we call an instance prompt) —not because it memorized this mapping, but because the France feature flows through the same invariant direction regardless of the surface form.
L279: We compare three approaches that leverage this insight, each with different tradeoffs between simplicity and expressiveness. All three methods perform classification using the Identity-Projection operator (Definition cite110†3.11 ), projecting the query onto normalized class directions. They differ only in how representations are transformed before projection. All probes operate on individual attention-head outputs, and we evaluate each attention head independently.
L280: #### Zero-Shot Probe.
L281: 
L282: The most direct instantiation of the Self-Reference Property is to use class-token hidden states themselves as class directions, without any training. To isolate class-specific components, we mean-center the token representations to remove features shared across all classes (e.g., “being a country”):
L283:  | $$\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{k}=\frac{\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}}{\|\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}\|},\quad\bar{\mathbf{h}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbf{h}_{t_{j}}.$$  |  | (7)
L284: 
L285: Classification is then performed by projecting instance representations onto these normalized directions. This procedure requires no training data.
L286: #### Unsupervised Probe.
L287: 
L288: We train a lightweight linear probe that aligns instance activations with class-token directions using only class tokens. Given an instance activation $\mathbf{h}$ and class-token prototypes $\{\mathbf{c}_{k}\}$ from the same head, the probe learns a transformation $W$ by minimizing the contrastive objective
L289: 
L290:  | $$\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{k}\log\frac{\exp((W\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}})^{\top}\mathbf{c}_{k}/\tau)}{\sum_{j}\exp((W\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}})^{\top}\mathbf{c}_{j}/\tau)}.$$  |  | (8)
L291: Crucially, $W$ is trained using only class tokens—no instance labels are used. The Self-Reference Property predicts that this transformation should generalize: if tokens and instances share invariant directions, orthogonalizing tokens automatically orthogonalizes instances. Table cite111†2 confirms this—the unsupervised probe matches or exceeds zero-shot performance despite never observing instances during training.
L292: #### Sparse Autoencoder Probe.
L293: We train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on attention-head outputs to learn reusable latent features in an unsupervised manner (cite71†Cunningham et al., 2023 ; cite70†Bricken et al., 2023 ; cite112†Kissane et al., 2024 ). Given an attention output $\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, the encoder produces sparse latents $\mathbf{z}=\mathrm{TopK}(W_{\mathrm{enc}}\mathbf{h}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{enc}})$ and reconstructs $\hat{\mathbf{h}}=\mathbf{z}W_{\mathrm{dec}}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}$.
L294: SAEs are trained only on implicit instance activations (no class tokens). Consistent with our theory, many SAE features activate for both class tokens and semantically related instances, indicating that SAEs recover the same invariant directions as token-based probes.
L295: #### Unified Classification.
L296: 
L297: For all methods, let $\phi(\cdot)$ denote the transformation (mean-centering, $W$, or SAE encoder). Classification uses the Identity-Projection operator with respect to the chosen class vectors:
L298: 
L299:  | $$\hat{k}=\argmax_{k\in[K]}\,\phi(\mathbf{h}(c))^{\top}\hat{\phi}_{k},\quad\text{where }\hat{\phi}_{k}=\frac{\phi(\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}})}{\|\phi(\mathbf{h}_{t_{k}})\|}$$  |  | (9)
L300: The query is not normalized, so projection magnitude reflects feature strength. Strong classification across all methods would confirm that the invariant structure from Theorem cite98†3.7 is recoverable through multiple independent approaches—providing converging evidence for directional invariance and the Self-Reference Property.

L334: ### 5.1 Datasets
L335: 
L336: We evaluate mainly across all the attention head outputs, on eight classification tasks spanning diverse semantic domains (Table cite113†1 ): taxonomic (Animals), geographic (Countries), affective (Emotional Sentences (cite114†Ghazi et al., 2015 )), stylistic (Literary Quotes, Cartoon Phrases), and linguistic (Languages (cite115†Artetxe et al., 2020 )) and descriptive (Fruits, Companies).
L337: For each task, we obtained a list of implicit sentences that express the class without mentioning it (e.g., “the country of the Eiffel Tower”). The full description of the datasets can be found in the Appendix cite58†D.1 .
L338: 
L339: The Fruits and Companies datasets test behavior under polysemy (Section cite32†5.3 ). Our geometric analysis uses LLaMA3-8B, while classification results span four model families (Table cite111†2 ) to demonstrate generalization.
L340: ### 5.2 Classification Results
L341: 
L342: We do not aim to determine which method is best, but rather whether invariant directions alone support zero-shot and unsupervised classification. Table cite111†2 presents classification accuracy across methods, models, and semantic domains. Several findings emerge.

L419: ## Appendix A Proofs of Main Results
L420: 
L421: ### A.1 Proof of Theorem cite98†3.7 (Invariant Subspace Necessity)
L422: ###### Proof.
L423: 
L424: Let $W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ be the linear interface (either $W_{U}$ for unembedding or $W_{O}W_{V}$ for attention). By Definition cite146†3.4 , there exists a linear functional $\boldsymbol{\phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ such that the $f$-relevant output is:
L425: 
L426:  | $$o_{f}(c)=\boldsymbol{\phi}^{\top}W\mathbf{h}(c)=\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c)$$  |  | (10)
L427: 
L428: where $\mathbf{w}_{f}=W^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$.
L429: Step 1: Equivalence class structure. Partition contexts by their required $f$-output. For contexts $c_{i},c_{j}$ requiring identical outputs ($o_{f}(c_{i})=o_{f}(c_{j})$):
L430: 
L431:  | $$\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c_{i})=\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c_{j})\implies\mathbf{h}(c_{i})-\mathbf{h}(c_{j})\in\ker(\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\top})=\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\perp}$$  |  | (11)
L432: That is, contexts with the same feature value can differ arbitrarily in directions orthogonal to $\mathbf{w}_{f}$, but must agree on their projection onto $\mathbf{w}_{f}$.
L433: 
L434: Step 2: Decomposition. For any context $c$ expressing $f$, decompose:
L435: 
L436:  | $$\mathbf{h}(c)=\mathbf{h}_{f}(c)+\boldsymbol{\eta}(c)$$  |  | (12)
L437: where $\mathbf{h}_{f}(c)$ is the $f$-relevant component satisfying $\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{f}(c)=o_{f}(c)$, and $\boldsymbol{\eta}(c)\in\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\perp}$ captures $f$-irrelevant variation. This decomposition is unique given the constraint.
L438: 
L439: Step 3: Invariant subspace construction. The $f$-relevant components $\{\mathbf{h}_{f}(c_{i})\}$ must satisfy $\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{f}(c_{i})=o_{f}(c_{i})$ for all $i$. Define:
L440:  | $$\mathcal{S}_{f}=\mathrm{span}(\{\mathbf{h}_{f}(c):c\text{ expresses }f\})$$  |  | (13)
L441: 
L442: This subspace satisfies the required properties:
L443: 
L444:   1. 1.
L445: 
L446: Context-invariance: $\mathcal{S}_{f}$ is determined by feature $f$ and the linear interface $W$ (through $\mathbf{w}_{f}$), not by any individual context.
L447: 
L448:   2. 2.
L449: 
L450: Completeness: By construction, $\mathcal{S}_{f}$ contains all $f$-relevant information from any context expressing $f$.
L451: 
L452:   3. 3.
L453: Minimality: The subspace is the span of $f$-relevant components, excluding $f$-irrelevant variation in $\mathbf{w}_{f}^{\perp}$.
L454: 
L455: The key insight is that the linear interface $W$ acts as a bottleneck: to produce consistent outputs for the same feature value across different contexts, the model must encode $f$-relevant information in a subspace that projects identically through $\mathbf{w}_{f}$. This subspace exists by construction and is independent of which specific contexts are considered. ∎
L456: ### A.2 Proof of Proposition cite107†B.2 (Dimensional Bound)
L457: ###### Proof.
L458: 
L459: By Theorem cite98†3.7 , there exists a context-invariant subspace $\mathcal{S}_{f}$ containing all $f$-relevant information. We show that linear separability of $K$ feature values constrains $\dim(\mathcal{S}_{f})\leq K-1$.
L460: Let $\{\mathbf{h}_{y_{k}}\}_{k=1}^{K}\subset\mathcal{S}_{f}$ be representative embeddings (e.g., class centroids) for each feature value $y_{k}$. For these to be linearly separable, they must be affinely independent: no $\mathbf{h}_{y_{k}}$ lies in the affine hull of the others.
L461: 
L462: The affine hull of $K$ points has dimension at most $K-1$. To see this, define centered representations:
L463:  | $$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{y_{k}}=\mathbf{h}_{y_{k}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}},\quad\text{where }\bar{\mathbf{h}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{h}_{y_{k}}$$  |  | (14)
L464: 
L465: These centered vectors satisfy $\sum_{k}\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{y_{k}}=\mathbf{0}$, so at most $K-1$ are linearly independent. Thus $\mathrm{span}(\{\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{y_{k}}\})\leq K-1$.
L466: Since linear separability requires the $f$-relevant subspace to distinguish all $K$ values, and this can be achieved in $K-1$ dimensions, the minimal invariant subspace satisfies $\dim(\mathcal{S}_{f})\leq K-1$.
L467: 
L468: For binary features ($K=2$), this bound yields $\dim(\mathcal{S}_{f})\leq 1$. Combined with the requirement that $\mathcal{S}_{f}$ be non-trivial (the feature must be detectable), we have $\dim(\mathcal{S}_{f})=1$, establishing directional invariance. ∎
L469: ## Appendix B Capacity Constraints and Feature Factorization
L470: 
L471: ### B.1 Detailed Proof of Proposition cite147†3.8 L472: 
L473: We provide a complete argument that capacity constraints in transformers force factorized representations with shared, invariant feature directions.
L474: ###### Proposition (Capacity Constraint Implies Feature Sharing, restated).
L475: 
L476: Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a transformer with vocabulary $|\mathcal{V}|$ and hidden dimension $d$, where $|\mathcal{V}|\gg d$. Under the following conditions:
L477: 
L478:   1. 1.
L479: 
L480: Linear readout: Token logits are computed via $\textup{logit}_{t}=\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c)$
L481: 
L482:   2. 2.
L483: 
L484: Sparse activation: Each context $c$ expresses a small subset of all possible features
L485: 
L486:   3. 3.
L487: 
L488: Shared features: Multiple tokens share semantic attributes
L489: Then the optimal representation factorizes tokens as:
L490: 
L491:  | $$\mathbf{w}_{t}=\sum_{f\in F_{t}}\alpha_{t,f}\,\mathbf{d}_{f}$$  |  | (15)
L492: 
L493: where $F_{t}$ is the feature set for token $t$, and $\{\mathbf{d}_{f}\}$ are shared feature directions with $|F|\ll|\mathcal{V}|$.
L494: ###### Proof.
L495: 
L496: We proceed in four steps, establishing that factorization is optimal under capacity constraints when features are sparse.
L497: #### Step 1: Dimensional constraint.
L498: 
L499: The hidden dimension $d$ bounds the number of orthogonal directions available. With typical values $|\mathcal{V}|\approx 50{,}000$ and $d\approx 4{,}000$, at most $d$ tokens can have mutually orthogonal representations in $W_{U}$. The remaining $|\mathcal{V}|-d$ tokens must share directions with others, which creates potential interference in the readout.
L500: #### Step 2: Interference cost depends on co-occurrence.
L501: 
L502: Suppose tokens $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ share a direction $\mathbf{d}$, i.e., both $\mathbf{w}_{t_{1}}$ and $\mathbf{w}_{t_{2}}$ have non-zero projections onto $\mathbf{d}$. Interference occurs when both tokens are relevant predictions for a context $c$: the hidden state $\mathbf{h}(c)$ cannot independently modulate the logits for $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ along their shared direction. The expected interference cost is:
L503:  | $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{interference}}(t_{1},t_{2})\propto P(t_{1},t_{2}\text{ both relevant in }c)\cdot|\mathbf{w}_{t_{1}}^{\top}\mathbf{d}|\cdot|\mathbf{w}_{t_{2}}^{\top}\mathbf{d}|$$  |  | (16)
L504: 
L505: For sparse features—those with low co-occurrence probability across the corpus—this interference cost is small.
L506: #### Step 3: Factorization minimizes total representation cost.
L507: 
L508: Consider the total cost of a representation as the sum of dimensional cost (number of directions used) and interference cost. Compare two strategies:
L509: 
L510:   * •
L511: 
L512: Unique directions: Each token $t$ receives a dedicated direction $\mathbf{d}_{t}$. This eliminates interference but requires $|\mathcal{V}|$ dimensions—infeasible when $|\mathcal{V}|\gg d$.
L513: 
L514:   * •
L515: Factorized features: Tokens share $|F|$ feature directions, where each token $t$ is represented as a sparse combination of features $f\in F_{t}$. This requires only $|F|$ dimensions plus interference costs proportional to feature co-occurrence.
L516: When semantic features are sparse and $|F|\ll|\mathcal{V}|$, the factorized strategy achieves lower total cost. Intuitively, “mammal” and “European” rarely co-occur as the dominant semantic features of a context, so tokens sharing these directions (e.g., “cat” and “France”) experience minimal interference despite their shared structure.
L517: #### Step 4: Each factor is communicable and invariant.
L518: 
L519: Under factorization, the logit computation for token $t$ decomposes as:
L520: 
L521:  | $$\text{logit}_{t}=\mathbf{w}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c)=\sum_{f\in F_{t}}\alpha_{t,f}\,\mathbf{d}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c)=\sum_{f\in F_{t}}\alpha_{t,f}\,\phi_{f}(c)$$  |  | (17)
L522: where $\phi_{f}(c)=\mathbf{d}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(c)$ is the activation of feature $f$ in context $c$. For the model to correctly predict token probabilities, the hidden state $\mathbf{h}(c)$ must encode each relevant feature $f$ such that $\phi_{f}(c)$ reflects the appropriate magnitude.
